proposal.description_short: Birthright citizenship executive order and later court injunction
proposal.description_medium: President Donald Trump signed the birthright citizenship executive order on January 20, 2025. It covered births where the mother was unlawfully present, or lawfully present temporarily, and the father was neither a U.S. citizen nor lawful permanent resident; the order exempted children of lawful permanent residents. proposal.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies not to recognize U.S. citizenship for certain children born in the United States. The order covered births when the mother was unlawfully present, or lawfully present temporarily, and the father was neither a U.S. citizen nor a lawful permanent resident; it expressly exempted children of lawful permanent residents. It was scheduled to apply to births more than 30 days after signing. The order’s signing and its later court challenges are separate milestones. Reuters reported that a Maryland federal judge issued a class-action injunction on August 7, 2025, the fourth nationwide injunction against the policy. The Supreme Court’s June 27 decision limited universal injunctions but did not decide whether this order complied with the Constitution. The cited records do not establish the held synopsis’s broad “neither parent” paraphrase, an annual estimate of 150,000 affected births, or an October 3 ruling date; those claims are omitted.

It does not say that the policy expressly directed family separation, state an intent to deter migration through separation, or establish the scale or duration of family separations. The release ties the policy to prosecution of unlawful-entry referrals under 8 U.S.C. § 1325(a), subject to prosecutorial resources.

proposal.title: Trump Urges Supreme Court to Limit Nationwide Injunctions
proposal.description_short: On March 20, 2025, Trump urged the Supreme Court to curtail federal judges’ power to issue nationwide injunctions blocking administration actions.
proposal.description_medium: On March 20, 2025, President Donald Trump urged the Supreme Court to curtail federal judges’ ability to issue nationwide injunctions against administration actions. Reuters reported that Trump posted “STOP NATIONWIDE INJUNCTIONS NOW” and that the Justice Department had asked the Court to narrow injunctions blocking his birthright-citizenship order. This supports a specific challenge to nationwide injunctions, not a claim that Trump denied courts all authority over the executive branch.
proposal.description_long: On March 20, 2025, President Donald Trump called on the Supreme Court to limit federal judges’ authority to issue nationwide injunctions blocking administration policies. Reuters reported that Trump made the appeal in a social-media post, writing “STOP NATIONWIDE INJUNCTIONS NOW,” and that the Justice Department was separately asking the justices to narrow three nationwide injunctions against his birthright-citizenship order. The cases involved courts in Washington state, Massachusetts and Maryland. Trump’s statement concerned the scope of injunctions that apply beyond the parties before a court. The available reporting does not say that he declared federal judges had no authority to constrain or review the executive branch. Reuters also reported that federal courts were hearing more than 100 lawsuits against administration initiatives and that the Supreme Court’s six-member conservative majority included three Trump appointees. Injunctions against earlier presidents had also been issued. The event should be described as a call to curtail nationwide injunctions and related Supreme Court litigation, not a rejection of judicial review generally.
